248.t: Blaze Away band, Harold Dejan and living uptown
248.s: Dawson refers Collins to Harold Dejan for the downtown Creole band, and says he grew up in the Third Ward around Perdido.
248.ch: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
248.q: Downtown, I'll tell you now, I'll tell you who can probably give you a little more idea about that band, more better than me, cause he'd come down the Creole part of the town. That's, uh, uh, what you call, uh, Harold. Harold Dejon.

248.t: Born in the French Quarter and moving uptown to Miro and Bolivar streets
248.s: Dawson was born downtown on Decatur between Esplanade and Barracks, attended a Catholic school until third grade, then the family moved uptown.
248.ch: Early life and the Whitney Bank
248.q: Uh, down, down in the French course at, uh, on St. Mary, uh, uh, by the, by the, between, uh, uh, Espenade, uh, on Decatur between, uh, uh, Charlize and, uh, I mean, on the trail between Espanade and Barracks.

619.t: Growing up in the 7th Ward among the Tios, Picou and Big Eye
619.s: He was born at Prairie and La Perouse and lists which street corners Big Eye Louis, Picou and the Tios lived on.
619.q: In the 7th Ward. That's why I moved back down here. I'm born right there. Prairie and La Perouse. You heard Big Iloy? Oh yes you heard man. I was living in the middle of the block. Big Iloy was living at that corner. Pico was living around the corner. Lorenzo Teo was living two blocks from me. Papa…

619.t: Neighbours of his boyhood and where musicians lived
619.s: Old man Glenn, Joe Brown and Manuel Perez lived near him, and he cannot place George Field's residence.
619.q: But I had old man Glenn in my band for years. But he was way older man than me. Why? Because old man Glenn was living a half a block from me. Oh, yeah. Oh, Joe Brown, another great bass player. He was just living a half a block from me also. I had all good musicians around my house. Manuel Perez,…

279.t: Birth and neighborhoods of New Orleans
279.s: Hug gives his birth date and the wards he grew up in, and the interviewer checks where the Irish Channel was.
279.q: I was born December the 6th, 1910, somewhere on Tulane Avenue. My father's memory is a little hazy now because he's very near 78. But it's somewhere around Tulane and Miro, I think. And I lived mostly around Bank Street. You might say the third ward, which took in Durgin Wall Street. And then later…

279.t: Born on Tulane Avenue, never leaving New Orleans
279.s: Hug explains he was born on Tulane Avenue, stayed in New Orleans, and grew up surrounded by street music.
279.q: That's right, John. I was born on Tulane Avenue. Dick is the one that told me this because I could never find out what street I was actually born on. But he knew it was somewhere on Tulane Avenue. And finally, my present wife was looking at some of the old photographs of my mother and father. And…

188.s: He first lived uptown in Carrollton, having gone to New Orleans in 1904 as a valet after his father took him out of school.
188.q: No, sir, I went down there first. I went down in 1904, October the 12th. Went down there as a valet. My father had taken me out of school and sent me down to the valet. What year did you went to the valet? Mr. McCaw, in 1904.

188.t: First years in New Orleans and the Tulane Band
188.s: He lived with Mr. McCall until his mother came, then with his brother met musicians, including Amos Riley's Tulane band.
188.q: when I first went down there with Mr. McCall I was living on Staten, Britannia that's a white neighborhood I was on premises and I stayed there with him until my mother came to New Orleans so I left I was too confined

681.t: Grandfather's property survey and old street maps
681.s: Hirsch shows the original surveyor's drawing of the Frenchmen and Decatur property with old street names and railroads.
681.q: Uh, we were talking about Lesion Fields. Here's something I have. From my grandfather's. I'm gonna have to get around here. Come around.

681.t: New Orleans summer breezes and air conditioning
681.s: A digression on breezes in New Orleans and in his house and how trees and building changed it.
681.q: In fact, that property that I got over on Bienville and Gaiosa. You go and open those two windows in that front room and it's the most delightful breeze at any time of the year.

638.t: Growing up in McDonoghville near George Lewis
638.s: He lived on the river side below Algiers near where George Lewis later lived.
638.q: I lived in New Orleans. But I lived on the other side of the river where I was born at down on the other side of the river in Algiers in McLendonville. That's right below Algiers. Down the coast they call it. Down there where George Lewis lived. Yeah.

638.t: Moving to New Orleans in 1923 and musician neighbours on St. Philip
638.s: He moved to St. Philip Street around 1923 and recalls where Kid Howard, Jim Robinson and Jim Hill lived.
638.q: Well, I moved over in Yarlene. When I moved to New Orleans, I moved to New Orleans in about 1923. Right before you started on the river.

199.s: Neighbours include James Rivers, Deacon Jones and Charles Moore.
199.ch: Growing up in the Thirteenth Ward
199.q: Oh, well, James Rivers. He's my neighbor. He lives on the corner. He's my neighbor right there. He's been up there about 12, 14 years on the corner. He moved up there. He came up there and found me at their address. He lives. The back of his house comes to like where you are. And I come out my side…

199.t: Birth and the Bell Castle Street houses
199.s: Born in New Orleans, he grew up in the Thirteenth Ward at 616 then 822 Bell Castle Street and later bought houses on the block.
199.ch: Growing up in the Thirteenth Ward
199.q: And then later on my mother, my mother was going to work one day and she worked at a place by the Bowman's family, Bowman's and Chapman's family on Valmont and Magazine. And she came out from Chapitool's to Walls Magazine and she saw a house at 822 Bell Castle, 1934. We moved from 616 to 822 Bell…

241.t: Where he lived: Clio Street, then across the river
241.s: He first lived on Clio Street, then moved across the river, where the photo was taken.
241.q: No, Clio Street. Oh yeah. I was on Clio Street when I first came here. Then I moved from Clio, then I moved on, uh, I went over the river and lived over the river.

245.t: Where Durand was born and Jimmy Noone's origins
245.s: The geography of St. Bernard Parish villages and that Noone was born where Durand was.
245.q: No, it was Merrillville. Merrillville. Merrillville. Merrillville. That's about three miles full, you get to Chip Allen Canal, which is called Violet. It's past Chalmette then.

999.t: Joseph Harris and the neighborhood of musicians
999.s: He names the snare player in the kazoo band and the old musicians who lived in his neighborhood.
999.q: He was a nice snap drum player too. He never did take any lesson or nothing. This guy around the street playing like I did. Maybe nobody got interested in the fall like they did me. Probably that's why they didn't get it. But he never played, you know.

474.t: Wallace Davenport's lessons and Jones's New Orleans house
474.s: Wallace Davenport's German teacher, and where Jones lived from 1925 and his mother's house.
474.ch: Donaldsonville, family and Richard M. Jones
474.q: Wallace took lessons from a German professor. Who did? They were still walking around here. In the 30's, because Wallace Davenport. Oh yeah. The German used to come over to the Wallace house with his little briefcase and teach Wallace. Wallace Davenport took lessons from a German professor. When…

899.t: Living on Bourbon Street and its renaming
899.s: He has lived near where he was born on Bourbon Street, which once ran to the lake and was renamed around 1936.
899.q: You know, I tell fellas, I say, I'm born on Bourbon Street, so some fellas would say, oh, he's just saying that Bourbon Street is famous.

254.t: Dixie, Johnson and Lincoln Parks: layout and where he lived
254.s: They place Dixie Park, Johnson Park and Lincoln Park close together and establish he lived on Short Street beside them.
254.q: Lincoln and, uh, Lincoln Park? What is it? Johnson Park. How far? Johnson Park was here and Lincoln Park. Just in your neighborhood? Lincoln Park was in one square and Johnson Park in this square right there where all them houses.

827.t: Where Arthur and his father were born and raised
827.s: Arthur was born by the Tremé Market, father born uptown near Burgundy Street, family later moved to Claiborne.
827.q: He was born up around Liberty Street somewhere. Uptown? Right, right, no, around Burgundy Street somewhere, towards Dumain. Where? That's where he was originally born.

773.t: Where she and her husband were born and raised
773.s: She was born on Tonti Street; her husband was raised by an aunt in the Tremé after his mother died.
773.q: Right here in New Orleans. Right here on Taunty between Tulane and the street coming this way. I think it's... Banks? Banks. And the house was just as good as if it was just built some years ago. You know, often I pass and I look at it, you know.

185.t: Birthplaces of Tio and his siblings
185.s: Tio and Lorenzo were born in New Orleans, on Caliborne and Roman, and the youngest sister was born in Bay St. Louis.
185.ch: Home life and the father's death
185.q: No, I'm born in the New Orleans. Right here. There was one that was born in Bay St. Louis and this is my youngest sister. Yes.

624.t: The house at 2119 Chippewa and the Irish Channel
624.s: They discuss the family home, the upstairs balcony where the band played, and the Irish Channel neighbourhood near the river.
624.q: There were a lot of good people. That's right. A lot of good. Self-made people. We were in the Jackson Avenue, you see.

150.t: Growing up in Algiers, Gretna and the Irish Channel
150.s: He lists the homes he lived in on both sides of the river, from Algiers and Gretna to 515 Third Street in the Irish Channel, and James Lewis School.
150.ch: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
150.q: Where? Well, I lived on both sides of the river. First, I was born on Tex Street in Algiers on the west bank of the river. And then my mother moved to, well, we were living in Gretna on the west bank of the river. I was on 5th Street right across from Hebe's Old Bakery where my mother and father…

1.s: Barker describes the tenement apartment at 1027 Charlotte Street where he lived until age six.
1.q: French Quarter, Ville Carrier. And the tenement. I'd say apartment building. New Orleans had apartment building with other people around. The country knew what they were. That's the folks who live in the law cabins. New Orleans had hair condition.

251.t: New Orleans without a wrong side of the tracks
251.s: Reel 2 begins with movie pianists, then neighbourhoods had no railroad-avenue divide and people rented homes.
251.q: In those days it weren't. I can't remember it being. Well, in other words, you're trying to see a segregating place as such as the other cities. No, yeah.

83.t: Moving to Governor Nichols Street and renaming the studio Cosmo
83.s: He left the jukebox, record and appliance businesses to become only a studio operator, renamed J&M Cosmo, and moved to 523-25 Governor Nichols, later adding 521.
83.q: well I moved because I got out of the jukebox business at that point I was no longer in the jukebox business I was no longer in the phonograph record business I was no longer in the appliance business I separated myself that was when I formally and finally and definitively became only a recording…

763.t: Where he lived and was born
763.s: He lived in the Quarter until about 30; he was born in Bayou St. John when luggers and schooners came in.
763.q: In fact, the time that I lived to be up until, I would say it, until I was up to 30 years old, I didn't move from Esplanade to Domaine. That was my quarters right there, from Esplanade to Domaine. No further up or no further down. Were you born right in that section? And from the riverfront to…

14.t: Early visits to New Orleans, living with a cousin
14.s: Love says he lived in New Orleans with a cousin by a canal as a boy.
14.ch: Early New Orleans and Plaquemine years
14.q: My cousin stayed there, Miss Bank. She's in G bamboo now. Mm-hmm. live right down on that canal there. What year was that you first started coming to town? That was way back. Maybe my wife might tell you the exact year, because she was born in Napoleonville, but she was raised up around there as a…

266.t: Living on Snipe Street in Lake Vista near Sharky
266.s: Jones says he lived on Snipe Street in Lake Vista, where streets have bird names, and Sharky lived not far away.
266.q: No, he wasn't that far away. I'm trying to think of anything. I don't know if it was Thrusher or some street like that he lived on.

601.t: George 'Shamrock' Stewart and living in Oakdale
601.s: Martin recalls visiting George Stewart, nicknamed Shamrock, with Russell, Slow Drag and George Lewis, and where those people lived in Oakdale. He says how long he has lived on this side of the river.
601.q: Yeah. I didn't know that. Yeah, you know the... Remember when we went over to his house? Me, you, slow-dragging... Wait a minute. George Lewis.

21.t: Hamilton Reynolds and Huey's house on Plum Street
21.s: Manetta recalls Hamilton Reynolds, head of the war board who oversaw street paying, and the house where he grew up.
21.q: At the Hamilton Reynolds house. Oh. I was a nice man, Hamilton Reynolds. He was a great friend of, well, he was a great friend of, he was the head of the board, the number two board of the war, number one world war and all that. Well, he's the, he had, he's the one who got all the streets, he was…

653.t: Growing up in the Seventh Ward melting pot of musicians
653.s: Born on Columbus Street near the brass band halls and the Autocrat, with musician families like the Pernells close by.
653.q: Oh I grew up in the Samoa, in the melting pot of musicians. Okay. I was born in 1623 Columbus Street. Okay. And that's right around the corner from the Burbank's and the Telus Falls and the Peters and the Jean-Jean-Me Hall where the brass bands met and the Artesian Hall where the brass bands met.…

403.t: Where Bolden grew up on First Street; his real name
403.s: Bolden grew up on First Street between Liberty and Howard; the interviewers' city directory lists Charles Bowen, which Jones confirms as his right name.
403.q: and there were two houses now on that block outside that corner house. Yeah. But, it's in the second house. The house right? On the corner house. Yeah. But, in the first side of that. Going out there.

706.t: Still living the early days; returning to New Orleans streets
706.s: He says he does not look back since he lives the same life, and enjoys the old neighborhood and its older women.
706.q: No, there wasn't no day to think back. I'm still living them. I still do the same thing. I mean, I eat my meals and I take care of my health and go and blow when I get ready to go to work and warm up and do the same thing.

44.s: Pete says he left Zachary for Baton Rouge in 1928 and describes the station stops.
44.q: Oh, yes. I've been moved away from Zachary, Louisiana since 28. And I've been around, let's say, Baton Rouge ever since. Yes. I was born and raised there in Zachary, but we left there in 28 and we've been living there in Baton Rouge.

46.t: Born on Liberty Street at the edge of the District
46.s: Wynn describes the block where he was born, on the edge of the District near Gravier Street.
46.q: I was born on Liberty Street between Tulane and Gravy. I don't remember the address. I thought it was, that's right on the edge of the district. At that time, the district was on Gravy Street. But this particular block on Liberty was a very nice block. Very nice, well kept and pretty flowers out…

152.t: Growing up on Bienville in the Fourth Ward
152.s: He describes the Bienville Street neighborhood near St. Louis Cemetery and who still lived at home.
152.q: between Galvis and Johnson. Uh, the fourth ward, which is very narrow. Mm-hmm. And width. Mm-hmm. Very long, all the way from the river, I think, to the lake. Mm-hmm. But it was the fourth ward. Mm-hmm. Really close to the St. Louis Cemetery. Okay. Uh, which was on Claiborne. Right. Uh, you could…

590.t: How New Orleans has changed; Alcorn's family roots
590.s: Alcorn says the city has changed for the better, describes his family born in New Orleans and the closeness of its people.
590.ch: The cancelled dance and race in New Orleans
590.q: All my days I was in New Orleans. When Calton was a town that saw me. This was a sexy town. My mother and them was in New Orleans. Not in Calton, they was in New Orleans. I didn't move up in Calton until... I had my family. Hmm. Twenty-some-odd years ago. Twenty-eight years ago. But that's the way…

121.s: Neighbors on Scott Street and by the Owl Club, and how open and safe the community was.
121.q: Or the... Let me see. Going way back, when we were living back on Scott Street, Reverend Ivy was the neighbor on one side, I can remember. And there was this lady who was living with my uncle, and he recently died. I'm talking about my uncle Bill. That's my mama's brother. Uh-huh. And it was a lady…

182.t: Early life in Algiers and Sox's Lane
182.s: He says he lived in Sox's Lane, far back from the later Navy station, where there were no halls.
182.q: I started playing, Sox's Lane, in the Navy. They got all that for the Navy now. Oh, now for the Navy. Yes. They didn't have no Navy there. Way down there.

48.t: Where Palmer grew up in New Orleans
48.q: No. Around the streets? Around up around Palmer's Avenue. My street. Palmer's Avenue. Howard. That's where I lived at. That's where I lived at. Was it named after some of your folks? Sure enough. No. It was named after another man. He was a doctor. Old doctor. And they named after him.

878.t: Childhood home and neighbor Buddy Bolin
878.s: He was born at 2319 First Street, moved to Third and Clara around age five or six, and later to Broadmoor. Harry relays what his brothers and half sister told him about Buddy Bolin, a fine cornetist who was confined as mentally ill and later played trombone; Russell gives his dates.
878.q: When we were... When I was about five or six years old, we moved to Third, Third and Clara. And we lived there up until about 1928. And we moved right back in Broadmoor, where I'm living now. Yes.

634.t: Birthplace, Dave Perkins and neighborhood parades
634.s: Happy was born on Dryades between Washington and Sixth; Dave Perkins lived nearby, and neighborhood parades were many.
634.q: And that's what my mother always told me. Uh-huh. And my mother, she was in the house after I got to be big. And she told me that where you was born.

192.t: Where the family lived in the Seventh Ward
192.s: He gives the addresses where he and his Marrero and Barnes relatives lived downtown.
192.q: Of all our life, that's easy, I was born 1123 Two Row Street. That's between Murray and St. Claude. Left from there we went in the next block, 1223 Two Row Street. And I stood there until I got married, January 31st, 1923.

50.t: Siblings who died young, yellow fever, her birthplace and homes
50.s: Few of the seven children lived; she was born on Frenchman Street and the family bought a home on St. Anthony Street.
50.q: And then you had yellow fever doing those days. Yeah. Because my grandmother lost a sister doing the yellow fever. Her name was Helena. Mm-hmm. But I don't remember—I don't believe my mother had any children to name but the three that she—that she sang. That's the three, yes, on the 100. And then…

194.t: Growing up downtown near Howard Avenue and Canal
194.s: He lived downtown between Howard and Canal near Dryades and Rampart; he says musicians simply gather wherever they can enjoy one another.
194.ch: Family and downtown New Orleans childhood
194.q: Well, really, you don't never know where the musicians be living at. I mean, they just all gather, drift around, and they get to the right places where they can enjoy one another, you know.

306.t: White Bear, Deku and the old trumpeter living on Burgundy Street
306.s: Talk of local musicians' hangouts and an elderly man still living on Burgundy Street whom Rene knew when he was young.
306.q: I saw a little dick named White Bear. He hangs in a burglar's spread out of the hood. Him and this fellow Deku. That's where they hang out. Every night if I want to find him to look him up.

831.t: Born on Magazine Street and musicians in the neighborhood
831.s: He was born at 1364 Magazine Street; the Majanas and Woodrow lived near him.
831.ch: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
831.q: I knew the Majotas lived right around the corner from me. Woodrow lived right around the corner from me.

138.t: The Charter Street basement house and rehearsals
138.s: Laine lived at about 2405 Charter near Mandeville in a basement house where the kids rehearsed.
138.q: It was a basement house. Mm-hmm. I lived in there for years and years. We used to rehearse it in the basement.

483.t: Sugar refinery job, Treme home and bandstand memories
483.s: Questions on Chris's jobs, where the family lived near Liberty and Treme, and Jack standing on the bandstand with his father.
483.q: you don't know the only job I remember that you know when he came when he first came he told me my uncle told me he worked in the iron you know that's all but in the wells I don't knew

885.t: Grandfather, birthplace and the St. Andrew Street neighborhood
885.s: Little known about grandparents; family origins, where he was born and raised, and the close-knit neighborhood.
885.q: God bless him. I never really had anything to him. Like I said, the family, the little records that they had. I couldn't tell you anything about that side of the family.

780.t: Growing up on South Robertson in the Garden District
780.s: He describes the neighborhood he lived in until about age 22.
780.q: Well, sort of up to the Garden District. And I was, I was born on South Robinson in the 1200 block. We, my family moved on the South street and I was, so they told me I was nine months old and they stayed there. I stayed there until I was about 22 years old. On the South street.

295.t: Living in the neighborhood and the volunteer fire companies
295.s: Jack has always lived in the same neighborhood and has belonged to the Davy Crockett volunteer fire company for about 45 years.
295.q: Right in this neighborhood all my life. From, say, Mandeville Street, which is only four squares from here, down to this hill, Clot Street. Uh-huh. In all my days I lived just in that same, in this same territory.

650.t: Birthplace and boyhood neighborhoods in New Orleans
650.s: Born on Calliope Street, he moved to Drive Street in the Garden District and later downtown to Padilla Street.
650.q: I was born on Caliope, between Rides and Barone. My native home. This is my native home. I left here. I left here. Went to California. But no, you're jumping ahead too far.

270.t: Looking at photographs of Donaldsonville streets and buildings
270.s: The interviewer shows pictures of Donaldsonville and Sayles identifies Railroad Avenue, the market and the Bank of Ascension.
270.q: Well, no, this is, yeah, yeah, I can see a little resembling here. Seemingly this is about near about the, yeah, that's the station here. I can see that.

574.t: Where Robinson lived on moving to New Orleans; Dave Perkins in white bands
574.s: His addresses on arrival and after 1921, and that Dave Perkins played with white bands.
574.q: No, just near Contoy. Not Contoy, Clio. Yes, I remember. Yeah, because the car used to go back there. And that's when you took lessons from Dave Perkins uptown, didn't you? Dave Perkins, yeah. Yeah. Yeah, I lived in the room then. Well, I think of Dave Perkins again. Was he playing in any band in…

307.t: Born on Taunty Street; neighborhood and later homes
307.s: He was born near Domaine and St. Anne, moved after marriage to Iberville and Gravier/Durbin for 18 years, and is back in the old neighborhood.
307.q: Well, when I got married, I got married on Iberville Street while I stayed up there quite a while. I moved up on Gravy and Durbin and I stayed up there about 18 years. But I'm back down in my old neighborhood where I was born and raised in the same neighborhood.

122.t: Introduction; how San Francisco has changed since the 1920s
122.s: Rowe opens the interview; Watkins describes ferries, bridges, districts, the Sunset's sand dunes and the postwar building boom.
122.q: Well yes. I’m a native born San Franciscan, I was born in 1920, January the 29th, and there have been many, many, many changes. Everything. Our skyline has changed, it’s been Manhattanized, our transportation system, which used to be the best in the country, we’re having problems with it. We went…

226.t: Spoiled only child in the family house on Touro Street
226.s: Grandparents, uncles and aunts lived together; the house is at 1240 Touro Street in the seventh ward and still stands.
226.q: I was spoiled. I was spoiled, and especially from my grandmother and grandfather. They – I could do no wrong with them. Being raised in a family where we all lived together – grandmother, grandfather, and even uncles and aunts all lived together – not everybody. Some lived in the same house, but…

493.t: Birth, Hickory Street home and the uptown neighborhood
493.s: Marsalis gives his birth details and the family house near Carrollton Avenue. He describes the mixed neighborhood and how New Orleans blocks are divided.
493.q: My full name is Jason Ignatius Marsalis. Date of birth is March 4th, 1977. I think at 5:30 pm Central Standard Time from what I understand. I was born in New Orleans, Louisiana.
